summary: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines admits most nationalities — including the EU, UK, US, Canada and the Commonwealth — visa-free for up to one month, extendable at the Immigration Department in Kingstown, while CARICOM nationals enter under Caribbean free movement and a short list of other countries needs a visa arranged in advance.

passportValidity.text: Carry a passport valid for at least 6 months on arrival. Visitors traveling on shorter validity are sometimes admitted if the passport covers the whole stay, but airlines apply the 6-month rule — do not rely on the exception.

source.name: Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — entry requirements
Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — entry requirements

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers aged 1 and over arriving from, or having transited more than 12 hours in, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission — relevant if you route through South America or West Africa. There is no requirement for arrivals from Europe, North America or the rest of the Caribbean.

source.name: Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — health requirements

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not required for entry and is not checked at the border. It is still worth holding: the Milton Cato Memorial Hospital in Kingstown handles routine care, but serious cases are flown to Barbados, Trinidad or Miami, and a medical evacuation from the Grenadines is expensive.

source.name: Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — entry requirements

onwardTicket.text: Immigration officers routinely ask visa-free visitors for a return or onward ticket and the address of your accommodation before granting the one-month entry stamp. Have both ready on the landing card.

source.name: Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — entry requirements

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published. Officers may ask visitors to show they can support themselves for the stay, particularly for longer visits or when accommodation is not pre-booked.

source.name: Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — entry requirements

declarations.name: Immigration and Customs Declaration Form
declarations.text: All arrivals complete a paper immigration and customs declaration card, usually handed out on the flight or the ferry. It asks for your accommodation address in Saint Vincent or the Grenadines — fill it in before you reach the desk.

source.name: Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — arrival procedures

currencyLimits.text: Cash of XCD 10,000 or more (or the equivalent in another currency) must be declared to Customs on arrival and departure under the country's anti-money-laundering rules.

source.name: Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — customs information

notes: Firearms, spearguns and ammunition may not be brought in without a permit issued in advance — this catches out yacht crews sailing down the Grenadines.
Fresh fruit, vegetables, plants, seeds and meat are controlled to protect local agriculture; declare anything of that kind rather than risk a fine.
Camouflage-pattern clothing is discouraged across the Eastern Caribbean and may be confiscated.

payments.text: Hotels, resorts and larger restaurants in Kingstown, Bequia and Canouan take cards, and ATMs dispense East Caribbean dollars. Carry cash for minibuses, ferries, market stalls and the smaller Grenadine islands, where card terminals are scarce and network outages are common. US dollars are widely accepted at a rate close to the fixed EC$2.70.

safety.text: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is a relaxed destination and violent crime rarely touches visitors, though petty theft from beaches, yachts and rental cars does happen. The bigger practical risks are natural: the La Soufrière volcano is active and monitored, and the June-to-November hurricane season brings storms and heavy swell.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: January to May is the dry season — steady trade winds, calm anchorages in the Grenadines and the lowest rainfall. Hurricane season runs June to November, with the highest risk from August to October.

tips.text: The official Atlantic hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30, peaking August to October. Ferries between the islands are canceled in heavy swell — build slack into island-hopping plans and check that your insurance covers weather disruption.

La Soufrière is an active volcano and erupted as recently as 2021. Hiking the crater is popular but follow the alert level published by the UWI Seismic Research Centre and the national emergency management organization (NEMO) before setting out.

Arriving by yacht you must clear immigration and customs at an official port of entry — Kingstown, Bequia (Port Elizabeth), Canouan, Union Island or Chatham Bay — before moving between the Grenadines.

If you want to stay beyond the month stamped in your passport, apply at the Immigration Department in Kingstown before it expires — extensions are routinely granted, but overstaying means a fine at the airport.
The EC dollar is pegged at EC$2.70 to US$1. Paying in US dollars is accepted almost everywhere, but you will usually get change in EC dollars and a slightly worse rate than the ATM.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Saint Vincent and the Grenadines?
faq.answer: Most travelers do not. Citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and most Commonwealth and Latin American countries enter visa-free for up to one month, extendable on request. CARICOM nationals enter under Caribbean free movement with up to six months. A limited list of nationalities — including several in Asia, the Middle East and Africa — must arrange a visa before traveling.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines?
faq.answer: Visa-free visitors are normally stamped in for one month, decided by the immigration officer at the border. You can apply at the Immigration Department in Kingstown to extend, typically in further one-month blocks up to six months in total.

faq.question: What applies to CARICOM citizens?
faq.answer: Under the Revised Treaty of Chaguaramas, CARICOM nationals arriving as visitors are entitled to a definite entry of up to six months, provided they have no adverse immigration record and can support themselves. Bring your CARICOM passport and be ready to state your address and length of stay.

faq.question: How do I get to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines?
faq.answer: Argyle International Airport (SVD) on Saint Vincent takes direct flights from Miami, New York, Toronto and regional Caribbean hubs, with connections through Barbados and Saint Lucia. The Grenadines are reached by inter-island ferry from Kingstown or by short flights to Bequia, Canouan, Mustique and Union Island.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate?
faq.answer: Only if you are arriving from — or have spent more than 12 hours in transit in — a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, which mainly means parts of South America and sub-Saharan Africa. Arrivals from Europe, North America and the rest of the Caribbean need no certificate.

faq.question: Can I enter by yacht without a visa?
faq.answer: The visa rules are the same by sea as by air — what changes is the procedure. The captain must clear the whole crew in at an official port of entry, present passports and the ship's papers, and pay cruising and port fees; each crew member gets the same entry stamp they would receive at the airport.
